strengths: Addresses genuine gap in psychiatric AI evaluation by moving beyond exam-style fact recall to real-world clinical decision-making tasks
Rigorous expert-driven dataset design with 9 practicing psychiatrists and no LM-generated content, avoiding synthetic data contamination
Sophisticated annotation processing using hierarchical Bradley-Terry model that captures annotator-specific biases and legitimate expert disagreement
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 15 models with multiple paradigms (multiple-choice, free-form) and systematic demographic bias analysis
Strong ethical reflection including thoughtful impact statement, acknowledgment of deployment risks, and discussion of bias mitigation
Open science commitment with public dataset (MIT license) and processing code enabling reproducibility and customization
weaknesses: Small dataset size (203 questions, uneven distribution with 28-50 per category) limits statistical power; triage/documentation confidence intervals overlap random baseline for open-source models

Incomplete validation: inter-rater reliability not reported for diagnosis/treatment/monitoring categories despite claiming 'only one correct answer'; process for designating best answers in ambiguous categories under-specified

Ambiguity handling creates tension—paper claims to capture ambiguity but designates single correct answer for triage/documentation; post-processing to set wrong answers to 0 probability applied post-hoc and could bias HBT estimates

Demographic bias findings show modest effect sizes (3% absolute differences) with overlapping confidence intervals and inconclusive annotator gender analysis; lacks causal investigation into observed biases
No human performance baseline despite this being standard in ML benchmarking and essential for interpreting whether 82% (diagnosis) or 44% (triage) accuracy is concerning

Evaluation results largely confirm expected patterns (larger models > smaller, closed-source > open-source) without surprising insights; mental health fine-tuning underperformance receives only brief discussion despite being notable
Limited methodological novelty—hierarchical Bradley-Terry is established technique; prompting and free-form evaluation use existing methods
U.S.-centric scope (9 U.S. psychiatrists, age 18-65 only) severely limits generalizability to other healthcare systems and patient populations
Free-form evaluation limited to 3 of 5 categories with indirect metric (1-BERTScore); Table 3 shows high 'inconsistency' even for 95%+ MCQA accuracy, raising questions about metric validity

strengths: Expert-created dataset addressing critical gap in psychiatric AI evaluation; clinician-designed without LM assistance across 203 carefully-verified questions spanning genuine clinical tasks (diagnosis, treatment, triage, monitoring, documentation)

Sophisticated dataset design with hierarchical Bradley-Terry model for handling ambiguous categories and systematic demographic parameterization (gender, ethnicity, age) enabling controlled fairness studies

Comprehensive evaluation of 21 models with multiple paradigms (task accuracy, demographic bias analysis, free-form consistency) and rigorous statistical treatment (bootstrap uncertainty quantification)
Systematic documentation of statistically significant demographic biases across all tasks and models (e.g., +10% male advantage in monitoring/documentation, +5-11% ethnicity variations)
High-quality annotation procedures with diverse annotators (9 question creators, 8 annotators from varied ethnic/gender/sexual orientation backgrounds) and transparent conflict resolution via debate
Strong reproducibility commitment: code, data, and detailed methodology publicly available (MIT license); extensive appendices enable modification and reproduction
weaknesses: Small dataset size (203 base questions; only 28-50 per category) limits discriminative power and generalizability; high per-category uncertainties (±0.14-0.20 in accuracy); constrains statistical conclusions and training utility

Validity concerns for triage and documentation categories: all models achieve ~44-51% accuracy (near 20% random baseline); qualitative error analysis reveals 'no clear pattern' in failures, raising questions about category soundness
Limited novelty: confirms existing knowledge that LLMs exhibit demographic biases (well-documented in prior work); no investigation of causal mechanisms or actionable mitigation strategies

Weak free-form evaluation methodology: BERTScore with fixed embeddings has known limitations; textual similarity to expert answers doesn't validate clinical correctness; authors acknowledge high-inconsistency but correct responses due to format differences, indicating poor metric calibration

Annotation quality uncertainties: no inter-rater reliability (Cohen's κ, Fleiss' κ) reported for single-answer categories (50% of data); Krippendorff's α ranges 0.0-0.8 for ambiguous questions; conflict resolution via 'debate' undocumented; post-hoc manual zeroing of 'objectively wrong' answers introduces subjectivity

Demographic bias in annotations unexplored: no analysis of whether diverse annotators actually improved quality; whether annotators' own demographics affected answers; whether psychiatric stigma in annotations is reflected in data

Fairness analysis is descriptive not causal: cannot determine if biases reside in models or in questions/reference answers; multiple comparisons (30+) without correction; age binned post-hoc into arbitrary ranges losing information

Practical impact limited: identifies biases but offers no mitigation strategies, model improvement guidance, or clinical deployment recommendations; narrow US-centric scope (DSM-5-TR, CPT codes) limits international applicability
